The binding, taught — how a browser tab live-switches hosts

Pedagogy·seedling·JUL 06, 2026

A plain-words primer on kolu's client-side binding layer — what a binding is, why switching hosts is hard, and the three bugs the design had to eat (the yank, the misroute, the toast leak) — ending at the framework primitives W4 extracted.

Contents

  • A binding is one tab’s live wire to one host
  • Why switching is genuinely hard (three ways to get it wrong)
  • The primitives (what the framework now owns)
  • The through-line, if you read both notes

This is the companion to the hosting side, taught. That note taught the server half — how a surface crosses a machine and how kolu-server holds a session per host. This one teaches the browser half: what happens in your tab when you switch which host you’re looking at, live, with no page reload. It ends where the last one did — at real primitives and the real bugs that shaped them — so you can read it cold and then judge the design.

The one-line orientation: the server holds N warm connections; the browser holds N too, with exactly one active — and “switch host” means swap which one is active without the page ever reloading. Everything below is what that swap has to get right.

A binding is one tab’s live wire to one host

When your browser talks to a host’s padi, a bundle of live things rides one websocket: the mirrored surface (terminals, cells), the streams (your terminal’s screen), the connection status. Pre-switch, that bundle was a module global — created once when the page loaded, pinned to window.location.host, and it lived exactly as long as the page. That buried assumption — the wire lives as long as the tab — is the thing the whole switch had to break.

A binding is that bundle, made first-class and plural: one per host (?host=zest on the same kolu-server), each with its own socket, its own status, its own teardown. A signal — activeHost — picks which one your tab is currently looking at. Switching is: point the signal at a different binding.Bindings are per-tab, deliberately: your laptop tab can sit on zest while your phone sits on sincereintent against the same kolu-server, neither disturbing the other. That’s why the active host lives in sessionStorage (per browsing context), not localStorage (shared across tabs).

Why switching is genuinely hard (three ways to get it wrong)

“Point a signal at a different binding” sounds trivial. It isn’t, because three things happen concurrently and each has a failure mode a naive swap walks straight into:

Bug 1 — the yank (a slow pick committing late). Warming a new host means an ssh provision that can take seconds. If you pick zest (slow), then change your mind and pick local, a naive await hosts.add(zest); setActive(zest) will — seconds later, when zest’s warm finally resolves — yank your tab to zest, overriding the newer pick. The fix is a pick epoch: bump a counter as the very first statement of switchHost (before even the “already on this host?” early-return, so that re-picking your current host cancels an in-flight pick), and after every await, bail if myPick !== pickEpoch. Last pick wins, always.The subtlety that made this a real bug and not a textbook one: an in-flight ssh warm can resolve after you’ve moved on, and the naive guard (retire-on-commit) covers the common ordering but not the “re-pick the current host to cancel” gesture — which commits nothing, so nothing retires, so the stale pick sails through. The epoch, bumped before the early-return, is what closes that hole.

Bug 2 — the misroute (a call landing on the wrong host). When you switch away, the old binding’s socket is still open for a moment, and a call already in flight on it could resolve against the old host while your UI now shows the new one — a silent wrong answer. The fix is retirement: switching retires the old binding — closes its socket and stubs its send to throw a typed “retired by this client” error. A late call now fails loudly at a dead transport instead of misrouting. (Crucially, the error is typed and honest — early versions threw a generic “server restarted — reload” error, which was a lie for an intentional switch and fired three red toasts every time; see Bug 3.)

Bug 3 — the toast leak (a subscription that outlives its binding). This one is the deepest, and it hid behind the other two. Every readout in your tab (memory, host inventory, daemon status) is a subscription on the active binding. When you switch, those subscriptions must tear down and re-open against the new binding — otherwise a subscription still listening on the retired socket catches the retirement error and reports it (three red “server restarted” toasts on every switch, which is exactly what a user first hit). The naive assumption was “the reactive owner disposes them.” It didn’t: the subscriptions were wrapped in a detached reactive root whose disposer was discarded — so switching disposed the per-key owner but never the subscription, which leaked live past the switch. Every switch leaked all three. The fix realizes one invariant: a disposed subscription cannot report anything — tie the detached root’s disposer to the caller’s owner so disposal actually reaches the subscription’s abort, and pass the abort signal all the way into the stream so a pending read cancels at once.The honest debugging story: the first instinct was to filter the retirement error at the subscribe site (a band-aid — suppress the symptom). The question “why isn’t the abort signal already catching this?” is what exposed the real defect: the sub was never disposed at all. The band-aid would have left a live subscription leaking on every switch, invisibly. Naming the invariant — disposed means silent — is what turned a symptom-suppression into a structural fix.

The primitives (what the framework now owns)

Those three fixes generalized. Rather than live as kolu-specific cleverness, they were extracted into @kolu/surface-app — because the volatility they tame (a set of live connections where the active one swaps at runtime) is not padi-specific; it is exactly what any multi-connection client faces (drishti’s fleet view is the same shape). Three receptacles resulted:

  • createActiveConnectionManager<K, C> — the client-side twin of buildHostRegistry (which the hosting note taught as the server’s session-per-host map). It owns the keyed cache, the one-active rule, retire-on-switch (Bug 2), the pick-epoch (Bug 1), and the “server rejected this host” fallback. kolu plugs in only policy: how to make a connection, how to warm it (hosts.add), what to toast, where to fall back.
  • connectionScoped — a subscription factory keyed to a swappable connection: it re-runs with full teardown when the active connection changes, is populated synchronously (so the first render never sees undefined), and is owner-safe (Bug 3). This is the general form of the client’s old bindingScoped.
  • createKeyedRoot<K, T> — the tiny primitive under both: dispose-and-recreate a reactive root when a key’s identity changes. It had been hand-rolled twice (once in the binding layer, once in the surface-app provider’s build-info swap); extracting it gave the swap-teardown guarantee one tested home.

The payoff for kolu: its binding/ module shrinks to pure policy — which host, the picker, recents, sessionStorage. All the mechanism — the cache, the epoch, the retirement, the re-keying, the leak-proof disposal — lives in the framework, tested once, where the next multi-connection client inherits it for free.

The through-line, if you read both notes

The hosting note ended on a rule: when your thing won’t fit a framework slot, ask what the slot’s code actually does — if the behavior fits, widen the slot; if it genuinely differs, build your own. This note is the mirror image on the client: when you build app-local machinery that tames a hard volatility (here: connection lifetime racing user intent), name the receptacle it wants and graduate it — even at a population of one, because the review’s job is to make the candidate visible, not to force the extraction. The server grew buildHostRegistry; the client grew createActiveConnectionManager; together the framework now owns both halves of “a changing set of live connections,” and both apps write only policy on top.
